question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
It is raining cats and dogs means:
option_3: something that does not upset you
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. it is raining very heavily.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "It is raining cats and dogs" means to rain very heavily or torrentially. (मूसलाधार बारिश होना)
◦ Example: We couldn't go out yesterday because it was raining cats and dogs.

• The idiom likely originates from old English usage, where heavy storms sometimes washed dead animals into the streets, giving the impression that animals had fallen from the sky.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "there are showers" is incorrect because it describes light or intermittent rain, not the intense downpour meant by the idiom.

• Option 3: "something that does not upset you" is incorrect because this meaning is unrelated to weather or to any accepted sense of this idiom.

• Option 4: "it is drizzling" is incorrect because drizzling refers to very light rain, which is the opposite of the heavy rain implied by the idiom.

NOTE

• Other common weather-related idioms tested in SSC: "Come rain or shine" (whatever happens), "Save something for a rainy day" (to save for future hardship), and "Right as rain" (perfectly fine).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
He was quite violent in his behaviour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gentle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Violent" means using or involving physical force intended to hurt, damage or kill; extremely forceful or aggressive. (हिंसक/उग्र)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Gentle", meaning mild, calm, kind and non-aggressive in manner. (सौम्य/नम्र)
◦ Example: Despite the provocation, he remained gentle and composed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Crazy" means mad or foolish; it is not opposite in meaning to violent.

• Option 2: "Aggressive" is actually a synonym of violent (forceful, hostile), not its antonym.

• Option 4: "Savage" also means fierce and brutal, making it a synonym of violent, not an antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonym-antonym pairs frequently tested: Violent ↔ Gentle/Peaceful/Mild; Aggressive ↔ Passive/Docile; Savage ↔ Civilized/Tame.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence to fill in the blank.
We usually had ________ visitors dropping by, but now we have very less visitors.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. umpteen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "less" means a smaller amount or number; not much/many. (कम)

• Its antonym here is "umpteen", meaning very many, a large indefinite number of. (अनगिनत/बहुत सारे)
◦ Example: She has given umpteen excuses for being late.

• The blank requires a word meaning "many/plentiful" to contrast with "very less visitors" in the second half of the sentence, so "umpteen" fits the sense of "We usually had [many] visitors... but now we have very less visitors."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "insufficient" means not enough, which is close in meaning to "less", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "a handful of" means a small number, which is again similar to "less", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "slighter" means smaller in degree, which is also similar in meaning to "less", not opposite.

NOTE

• Other quantity-related synonym/antonym pairs: Umpteen/Plenty/Numerous ↔ Scanty/Meagre/Sparse; Abundant ↔ Scarce.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The man was convicted for murder by the jury but he is not committed it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. had not committed it.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The main clause "The man was convicted for murder by the jury" is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Sequence of Tenses: When the main/earlier action is in the Simple Past Tense and a second action refers to something that happened (or did not happen) even earlier than that, the Past Perfect Tense (had + V3) is used.

• Here, the man's not committing the murder is an action/state that precedes his conviction, so it must be expressed using the past perfect: "...but he had not committed it."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "have not committed it" is incorrect because "have" is a present perfect auxiliary and does not agree with the past tense of the main clause.

• Option 2: "has not committed it" is incorrect for the same reason — it is present perfect, inconsistent with the past tense of "was convicted".

• Option 4: "am not committed it" is incorrect because it uses the simple present auxiliary "am" with a third person subject "he", which is grammatically wrong, and also fails to fit the past sequence.

NOTE

• A common sequence-of-tense error is mixing present/present perfect auxiliaries with a past-tense main clause. Always check whether the subordinate action happened before, during, or after the main past action to choose Past Perfect, Past Continuous, or Simple Past accordingly.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Hardik's horoscope says / that the stars / will be exercised / a benign influence on his life.
option_4: a benign influence on his life
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. will be exercised.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence intends to say that the stars will exercise (have) a benign influence on his life — that is, the stars are the doer of the action of exercising an influence.

• Rule: When the subject itself performs the action of "exercising an influence", the verb must be in the active voice ("will exercise"), not the passive voice ("will be exercised"), because the subject "the stars" is not the receiver of the action but the doer.

• The erroneous passive construction "will be exercised a benign influence" should be corrected to the active form: "will exercise a benign influence".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Hardik's horoscope says" is grammatically correct — a simple present tense clause correctly introducing reported content.

• Option 3: "that the stars" is grammatically correct — a correctly formed noun clause connector introducing the subject "the stars".

• Option 4: "a benign influence on his life" is grammatically correct as a noun phrase in itself; the error lies specifically in the verb form preceding it, not in this phrase.

NOTE

• Watch for phrases like "exercise influence/control/caution/authority" — these are commonly used in the active voice; do not passivise them incorrectly. Compare: "exercise an influence" (correct) vs. "be exercised an influence" (incorrect).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Someone who dishonestly pretends to deceive under an assumed character
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Imposter.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "Imposter" is a person who pretends to be someone else in order to deceive others, especially for fraudulent gain. (धोखेबाज़/पाखंडी)
◦ Example: The police arrested an imposter who had been posing as a bank official.

• The phrase "dishonestly pretends...under an assumed character" precisely matches the sense of assuming a false identity to deceive, which is the core meaning of "Imposter".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Imitator" (नकल करने वाला): One who copies or mimics another; imitation need not involve dishonest deception of identity.

• Option 3: "Explorer" (खोजकर्ता): One who travels to discover new places; unrelated to deception.

• Option 4: "Imbecile" (मूर्ख): A stupid or foolish person; unrelated to pretending or deception.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: Hypocrite (one who pretends to have virtues/beliefs they do not have), Charlatan (a fraud who falsely claims special knowledge/skill).

question:
Select the grammatically correct sentence.
A.Today is sixth day of our workshop. All the participants are highly enthusiastic.
B. Today is a sixth day of our workshop. All the participants are highly enthusiastic.
C. Today is the sixth day of our workshop. All the participants are highly enthusiastic.
D. Today is sixth day of our workshop. All participants are highly enthusiastic.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. C. Today is the sixth day of our workshop. All the participants are highly enthusiastic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Ordinal numbers require the definite article "the": Ordinal numbers (first, second, sixth, etc.) used as adjectives before a noun must be preceded by the definite article "the", e.g., "the sixth day", not "a sixth day" or simply "sixth day".

• Rule — "All the + noun" vs. "All + noun": When referring to a specific, already-identified group (the participants of this particular workshop), the definite article "the" should be used: "All the participants", not the more general "All participants".

• Sentence C correctly uses both "the sixth day" and "All the participants", making it the only fully grammatically correct option.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (D): "Today is sixth day of our workshop. All participants are highly enthusiastic." is incorrect because it omits "the" before "sixth day" and before "participants".

• Option 3 (B): "Today is a sixth day of our workshop..." is incorrect because the indefinite article "a" cannot be used with an ordinal number like "sixth" — there can only be one "sixth day".

• Option 4 (A): "Today is sixth day of our workshop..." is incorrect because it omits the required article "the" before "sixth day".

NOTE

• Ordinals (first, second, third...) and superlatives (best, tallest...) almost always take "the": "the first prize", "the tallest building". Remember this rule for both error-spotting and sentence-improvement questions.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Was the conference not attended by them?
option_1: Did they not attend the conference?
option_2: Does they not attend the conference?
option_3: Do they not attend the conference?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Did they not attend the conference?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Was the conference not attended by them?" is a passive, interrogative, negative sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense (interrogative, negative):
◦ Passive: Was/Were + Subject + not + V3 + by + Agent?
◦ Active: Did + Agent + not + V1 + Object?

• Applying the rule: the agent "them" becomes the subject "they"; the auxiliary "was" becomes "did"; the past participle "attended" becomes the base form "attend"; and the object "the conference" remains as the object.
◦ Active: Did they not attend the conference?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Does they not attend the conference?" is incorrect — "Does" does not agree with the plural subject "they", and it also wrongly shifts the tense to present.

• Option 3: "Do they not attend the conference?" is incorrect because it changes the tense to Simple Present instead of retaining the Simple Past Tense of the original sentence.

• Option 4: "Do they attend the conference?" is incorrect because it drops the negation "not" entirely and also wrongly shifts the tense to present.

NOTE

• When converting an interrogative passive sentence beginning with "Was/Were" to active voice, the auxiliary "did" is used and the main verb reverts to its base (first) form. Always preserve both tense and negation during the conversion.

question:
Select the option that express the given sentence in active voice.
Was the beggar not being beaten by her?
option_1: Was not she beating the beggar?
option_3: Was the beggar beaten by her?
option_4: Was she not beating the beggar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Was she not beating the beggar?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Was the beggar not being beaten by her?" is a passive, interrogative, negative sentence in the Past Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense (interrogative, negative):
◦ Passive: Was/Were + Subject + not + being + V3 + by + Agent?
◦ Active: Was/Were + Agent + not + V1+ing + Object?

• Applying the rule: the agent "her" becomes the subject "she"; the auxiliary "was...being" becomes "was"; the past participle "beaten" becomes the present participle "beating"; and the object "the beggar" remains as the object, with the negation "not" retained.
◦ Active: Was she not beating the beggar?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Was not she beating the beggar?" is incorrect because the word order of "not" is wrong; in standard interrogative negatives with a pronoun subject, "not" follows the subject: "Was she not..." not "Was not she...".

• Option 2: "Was she beating the beggar?" is incorrect because it omits the negation "not" present in the original sentence, changing its meaning.

• Option 3: "Was the beggar beaten by her?" is incorrect because it remains in the passive voice (retains "by her" and the past participle "beaten") and also drops the negation.

NOTE

• For Past Continuous passive-to-active conversion, remember the object of the passive sentence becomes the subject of the active sentence, and "being + V3" becomes "V1+ing". Negation and question word order must be carried over accurately.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.
Neither John nor Simon are coming to the meeting.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. is coming to the meeting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Subject-Verb agreement with "Neither...nor": When two singular subjects are joined by "neither...nor", the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it (the "Rule of Proximity").

• Here, both "John" and "Simon" are singular, so the verb closer to the second subject "Simon" must also be singular: "is", not "are".

• The correct sentence is: "Neither John nor Simon is coming to the meeting."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "were coming to the meeting" is incorrect because "were" is a plural/past form; it does not correct the agreement with the singular "Simon" in this present continuous context.

• Option 2: "No substitution" is incorrect because the original sentence contains a clear subject-verb agreement error ("are" should be "is").

• Option 3: "are coming to meeting" is incorrect because it retains the wrong plural verb "are" and additionally drops the required article "the" before "meeting".

NOTE

• The Rule of Proximity also applies to "either...or" and "not only...but also" — the verb always agrees with the subject nearest to it. Example: "Either the teacher or the students are responsible."

question:
The given sentence has some words with incorrect spellings. Select the most appropriate option that corrects the spellings.
Being a milionaire, he is leading a luxurius life.
option_1: Being a millioneire, he is leading a luxrious life.
option_2: Being a millionaire, he is leading a luxurious life.
option_3: Being a millionaire, he is leeding a luxurous life.
option_4: Being a millinaire, he is leading a luxurious life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Being a millionaire, he is leading a luxurious life.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Millionaire" — a person whose wealth amounts to a million pounds, dollars, or other unit of currency.

• The correct spelling is "Luxurious" — extremely comfortable, elegant or expensive.

• Spelling key: Millionaire = MILLION + AIRE (not "eire" or a dropped letter); Luxurious = LUXURY + OUS, retaining the "i" before "ous" (not "luxrious" or "luxurous").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "millioneire" and "luxrious" are incorrect — "millioneire" wrongly places "eire" instead of "aire", and "luxrious" wrongly drops the "u" from "luxurious".

• Option 3: "leeding" and "luxurous" are incorrect — "leeding" is a misspelling of "leading", and "luxurous" wrongly drops the "i" from "luxurious".

• Option 4: "millinaire" is incorrect — it wrongly drops the second "l" from "million"; although "luxurious" in this option is spelt correctly, the sentence as a whole still retains the error in "millinaire".

NOTE

• Commonly misspelt words in SSC exams with similar patterns: entrepreneur, questionnaire, connoisseur (all involve tricky "-aire"/"-eur" endings); furious, curious, notorious (follow the same "-ous" ending pattern as luxurious).

question:
Select the option that is similar in meaning to the given word.
Hapless
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Unfortunate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hapless" means unlucky, unfortunate, having no luck. (अभागा/दुर्भाग्यपूर्ण)
◦ Example: The hapless victim lost everything in the flood.

• The word derives from "hap" (an old word for luck/chance) plus the suffix "-less" (without), literally meaning "without luck".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Happy" (खुश): Means feeling or showing pleasure; this is nearly opposite in tone to "hapless".

• Option 3: "Fortunate" (भाग्यशाली): Means lucky, which is the direct antonym of "hapless", not a synonym.

• Option 4: "Distasteful" (अरुचिकर): Means unpleasant or offensive to taste/feelings; unrelated to luck.

NOTE

• Other words built with "-less" meaning "without": Hopeless (without hope), Ruthless (without pity), Reckless (without care). Synonyms of hapless: unlucky, luckless, ill-fated, star-crossed.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I find that students nowadays are not interested in ________ letters by hand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. writing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a word meaning "to form letters or words on a surface using a pen/pencil", which is "writing".

• The other three options are homophones or near-homophones of "writing" but carry entirely different meanings: "righting" (correcting/setting upright), "rioting" (taking part in a violent public disturbance), "rating" (assigning a rank or score).

• Only "writing" logically completes the sense of the sentence: "students... are not interested in writing letters by hand."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "righting" is incorrect because it means correcting or restoring to an upright position, which does not fit "letters by hand".

• Option 2: "rioting" is incorrect because it means participating in a violent disturbance, unrelated to letters.

• Option 3: "rating" is incorrect because it means evaluating or scoring something, which does not fit the context of writing letters by hand.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophone sets tested in SSC: write/right/rite; there/their/they're; hear/here; peace/piece. Always check the meaning that fits the sentence, not just the sound.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Conspirasy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Conspiracy" — a secret plan by a group to do something harmful or illegal. The word "Conspirasy" given in Option 3 is incorrectly spelt.

• Spelling key: Conspiracy = CONSPIR + ACY (ends in "-acy", not "-asy"). Compare with other "-cy" abstract nouns like "accuracy", "privacy", "legacy".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Consultancy" is correctly spelt — a business providing expert advice, formed from "consult" + "ancy".

• Option 2: "Constitution" is correctly spelt — the fundamental principles/laws of a state or organisation.

• Option 4: "Configuration" is correctly spelt — the arrangement of the parts of something.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-acy" (conspiracy, accuracy, privacy, legacy, diplomacy) are frequently confused with a wrong "-asy" ending in SSC spelling questions — always double-check this specific ending.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given phrase.
Waver between different opinions or actions
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Vacillate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Vacillate" means to waver between different opinions or actions; to be indecisive. (हिचकिचाना/दुविधा में रहना)
◦ Example: He vacillated for hours before finally deciding which job offer to accept.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sway" (झुकाना/प्रभावित करना): Means to move slowly back and forth, or to influence someone's opinion — not the same as being indecisive oneself.

• Option 2: "Viaduct" (उपरिपथ): A long bridge-like structure carrying a road or railway over a valley; a completely unrelated concrete noun.

• Option 3: "Thrifty" (मितव्ययी): Means careful with money, economical; unrelated to indecision.

NOTE

• Words related to indecision often tested: Waver, Dither, Equivocate, Oscillate, Hesitate — all near-synonyms of "Vacillate".

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who looks at the negative side of everything
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Pessimist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Pessimist" is one who habitually looks at the negative or worst side of things; one who expects the worst outcome. (निराशावादी)
◦ Example: Being a pessimist, he always assumes the plan will fail.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Optimist" (आशावादी): One who looks at the positive/hopeful side of things — the direct opposite of "pessimist".

• Option 2: "Activist" (कार्यकर्ता): One who campaigns actively for social or political change; unrelated to outlook on life.

• Option 3: "Racist" (नस्लवादी): One who discriminates against people of a different race; unrelated to negativity in outlook.

NOTE

• Common antonym pair: Optimist ↔ Pessimist. Related one-word substitutes: Cynic (one who believes people are motivated purely by self-interest), Misanthrope (one who dislikes humankind).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Taking a bull by the horns
option_2: To decapitate a bull for beef
option_3: To make a stupid decision thinking it to be daring
option_4: To deal with a difficult situation in a very direct or confident way
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To deal with a difficult situation in a very direct or confident way.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To take the bull by the horns" means to confront a difficult or dangerous situation directly and with courage/confidence, rather than avoiding it. (साहसपूर्वक कठिनाई का सामना करना)
◦ Example: Instead of ignoring the problem, she took the bull by the horns and confronted her manager directly.

• The idiom draws its imagery from the risky act of literally grabbing a bull by its horns to control it — the most direct, courageous way to handle a dangerous animal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Wearing a skull cap" has no connection to the idiom's meaning; it is a literal, unrelated statement.

• Option 2: "To decapitate a bull for beef" is a literal, gruesome misreading of the idiom rather than its figurative meaning.

• Option 3: "To make a stupid decision thinking it to be daring" is incorrect because the idiom implies genuine courage and decisiveness, not foolishness.

NOTE

• Other idioms of courage/directness tested in SSC: "To face the music" (to accept the consequences of one's actions), "To bite the bullet" (to endure a painful situation bravely), "To stick one's neck out" (to take a risk).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Heavy outfits make the movement of trekkers sluggish.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Active.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "Sluggish" means slow-moving, lacking energy or alertness; inactive. (सुस्त/मंद)

• Its antonym is "Active", meaning energetic, lively, moving quickly. (सक्रिय/चुस्त)
◦ Example: After a good night's sleep, she felt active and ready for the trek.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Distorted" means twisted out of shape or misrepresented; it has no relation to speed or energy.

• Option 3: "Eye catching" means visually striking or attractive; unrelated to the idea of movement/energy.

• Option 4: "Comfortable" means physically at ease; while heavy outfits might reduce comfort, this is not the direct antonym of "sluggish" (which is about pace/energy, not comfort).

NOTE

• Other synonym-antonym pairs based on "energy level": Sluggish/Lethargic/Languid ↔ Active/Brisk/Energetic/Vigorous.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The family is neither interested in selling the house or rebuilding it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. nor rebuilding.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Correlative Conjunction "Neither...Nor": The conjunction "neither" must always be paired with "nor", never with "or".

• The given sentence uses "neither...or", which is grammatically incorrect; it must be corrected to "neither...nor": "The family is neither interested in selling the house nor rebuilding it."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "yet rebuilding" is incorrect because "yet" is not the correlative pair of "neither"; it disrupts the required "neither...nor" structure.

• Option 2: "not only rebuilding" is incorrect because "not only" pairs with "but also", not with "neither", and its meaning also does not fit the sentence.

• Option 4: "but also rebuilding" is incorrect for the same reason — "but also" is the correlative pair of "not only", not of "neither".

NOTE

• Other fixed correlative conjunction pairs frequently tested: either...or, not only...but also, both...and, whether...or. Mixing pairs (e.g., "neither...or", "either...nor") is a classic SSC error type.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym for the underlined word in the given sentence.
She had the temerity to call her teacher a liar.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. impudence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Temerity" means excessive confidence or boldness; audacity; reckless disregard for danger or consequences. (दुस्साहस/धृष्टता)
◦ Example: He had the temerity to question the judge's decision in open court.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "impudence", meaning bold disrespect; shameless audacity. (ढिठाई/धृष्टता)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "tedious" (उबाऊ): Means long, boring and tiresome; unrelated to boldness or audacity.

• Option 3: "taciturn" (मितभाषी): Means reserved or reluctant to speak; the opposite trait of boldly speaking out.

• Option 4: "trenchant" (तीक्ष्ण): Means vigorous or incisive in expression (e.g., trenchant criticism); it describes sharpness of speech/writing, not audacious boldness itself.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "temerity": audacity, effrontery, impudence, nerve, gall. Antonyms: timidity, diffidence, caution.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The (1)________ of climate change is one of the most pressing issues facing the world today. Rising temperatures, extreme weather events and melting ice caps are just a few of the (2)________ of a changing climate. To combat this, many countries have pledged to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, but progress has been slow. In addition, some people are still sceptical of the (3)________ of climate change or believe that it's a natural occurrence that humans can't do much about. However, scientists agree that urgent action is needed to prevent the worst impacts of climate change. This includes not only reducing emissions but also adapting to the changes that have already (4)________. This might involve building sea walls to protect against rising sea levels, planting drought-resistant crops or developing new technologies to remove carbon from the atmosphere. Ultimately, addressing climate change will require a (5)________ effort from individuals, governments and businesses around the world.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. challenge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes climate change as "one of the most pressing issues facing the world today", which logically means it must be presented as a "challenge" — a difficult problem requiring effort to overcome.

• The word must fit the sense of "climate change is a major problem/difficulty", which is precisely what "challenge" conveys.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "advantage" is incorrect because it means a benefit or favourable factor, which contradicts the passage calling this a "pressing issue".

• Option 3: "solution" is incorrect because climate change itself cannot logically be called a "solution" — it is the problem the passage discusses, not the fix for it.

• Option 4: "aspect" is incorrect because it means merely one part or feature of something, which does not carry the sense of difficulty or urgency required by "pressing issue".

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the full sentence (and often the surrounding sentences) to judge tone — here "pressing issue" strongly signals a word conveying difficulty, i.e., "challenge", rather than a neutral or positive word.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The (1)________ of climate change is one of the most pressing issues facing the world today. Rising temperatures, extreme weather events and melting ice caps are just a few of the (2)________ of a changing climate. To combat this, many countries have pledged to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, but progress has been slow. In addition, some people are still sceptical of the (3)________ of climate change or believe that it's a natural occurrence that humans can't do much about. However, scientists agree that urgent action is needed to prevent the worst impacts of climate change. This includes not only reducing emissions but also adapting to the changes that have already (4)________. This might involve building sea walls to protect against rising sea levels, planting drought-resistant crops or developing new technologies to remove carbon from the atmosphere. Ultimately, addressing climate change will require a (5)________ effort from individuals, governments and businesses around the world.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. consequences.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rising temperatures, extreme weather events and melting ice caps are all results or effects caused by a changing climate, which is precisely the meaning of "consequences".

• The sentence structure "just a few of the ________ of a changing climate" requires a word meaning "outcomes/effects", matching "consequences".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "benefits" is incorrect because rising temperatures and melting ice caps are harmful effects, not advantages, of climate change.

• Option 2: "advancements" is incorrect because it means progress or improvements, which does not describe harmful natural phenomena.

• Option 4: "improvements" is incorrect for the same reason — these phenomena represent deterioration, not improvement.

NOTE

• Words like "consequences", "effects", "outcomes", "repercussions" and "ramifications" are commonly interchangeable in such contexts and frequently tested together in SSC cloze passages.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. reality.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes people who "are still sceptical", i.e., doubtful, and who alternatively "believe that it's a natural occurrence" — meaning some people doubt that climate change is genuinely happening/real, or attribute it to nature.

• The word required must mean "the fact of something actually being true/existing", which is exactly "reality" — being sceptical of the reality of climate change means doubting that it truly exists or is human-caused.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "fiction" is incorrect because being "sceptical of the fiction" would mean doubting something already assumed to be false, which contradicts the sentence's logic.

• Option 2: "myth" is incorrect for a similar reason — one would not typically be "sceptical of a myth" (a myth is already understood as untrue); the sentence needs a word implying something that could be real.

• Option 4: "deception" is incorrect because it means a deliberate act of misleading someone, which does not fit the neutral scientific context of doubting climate change's existence.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, check whether the required word must pair logically with the surrounding verb (here, "sceptical of the ___"). "Sceptical of the reality" is a natural collocation, while "sceptical of the myth/fiction" is not standard usage.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. occurred.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a verb meaning "happened/taken place" to complete "the changes that have already ________", and "occurred" (past participle of "occur") is the natural fit: "the changes that have already occurred".

• Grammar point: Since the sentence uses the Present Perfect Tense ("have already ________"), the verb must be in its past participle (V3) form — "occurred" correctly fits this structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "ceasing" is incorrect because it is a present participle (-ing form), which does not fit the "have already ________" (present perfect) structure, and its meaning "stopping" does not fit the sense of changes having taken place.

• Option 2: "reversing" is incorrect for the same grammatical reason (an -ing form used incorrectly), and its meaning (turning back to a previous state) does not match "changes that have already ________".

• Option 4: "stabilising" is also an -ing form, grammatically inconsistent with "have already ________", and would suggest the changes are becoming steady, which does not fit the intended meaning of changes that have already taken place.

NOTE

• After "have/has/had", only the past participle (V3) form of the verb is used in the Present/Past Perfect Tense. Options ending in "-ing" (ceasing, reversing, stabilising) can be immediately ruled out in such Perfect Tense blanks.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. joint.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states the effort must come "from individuals, governments and businesses around the world" — that is, from multiple different parties acting together, which is precisely the meaning of "joint" (combined, done together by more than one party).

• A "joint effort" collocates naturally with a list of multiple contributing parties, matching the sentence's structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "individual" is incorrect because it means done separately by one person, which contradicts the sentence listing multiple collective parties (individuals, governments, businesses) working together.

• Option 3: "solitary" is incorrect because it means alone or single, which is the opposite of an effort involving many parties.

• Option 4: "separate" is incorrect because it means apart or disconnected, which again contradicts the collective, combined nature of the effort described.

NOTE

• Common collocations tested in SSC cloze passages: "joint effort", "collective responsibility", "combined initiative" — all imply cooperation among multiple parties, unlike "individual/solitary/separate" which imply isolation.
